bluf: The U.S.-Iran war, now in its fourth month, is cascading across continents: from an energy crisis in Southeast Asia to a deepening polarization of Muslim communities in the Philippines, to a fundamental realignment of trade and security alliances as partners hedge against U.S. unpredictability. Simultaneously, the erosion of ceasefire frameworks in Gaza and southern Lebanon, combined with Russian escalations near NATO borders and North Korean troop deployments to Ukraine, is driving a synchronized global rearmament cycle. The Trump administration's transactional approach—pausing Taiwan arms sales as a bargaining chip while waging an unauthorized war and pursuing tariff-driven economic nationalism—is fracturing long-standing alliance consensus and incentivizing rival blocs to accelerate their own technological and military build-ups.

sections.title: Energy Chokepoint Warfare and the Global Economic Contagion
sections.content: The U.S.-Iran conflict has transformed the Strait of Hormuz from a strategic chokepoint into an active war zone, with direct and measurable consequences across the Indo-Pacific and Europe. Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters announced on May 30 that all vessels must obtain permission from the IRGC Navy and comply with designated routes, effectively asserting unilateral control over the waterway. This follows a U.S. Navy blockade that, by mid-May, had turned around over 100 ships and cost an estimated $29 billion. The immediate economic shockwave hit the Philippines first: Manila declared a state of emergency as oil, LNG, and essential product shortages paralyzed the economy and triggered protests. The Philippines is now the canary in the coal mine for energy-dependent economies across Asia. Simultaneously, the conflict is tearing at the social fabric of Muslim-majority regions far from the theater. In the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region of the Philippines, the war has deepened a pre-existing sectarian divide between Shia-supporting and Sunni-critical scholars, threatening community cohesion. This pattern mirrors earlier fractures caused by the Abraham Accords and indicates that Middle Eastern proxy conflicts are now destabilizing Southeast Asian societies from within. The energy crisis also reverberates in Europe: a Russian drone strike on Galati, Romania—a major Danube port—on the same week underscores how multiple chokepoints (Hormuz, Black Sea, Russian pipelines) are being weaponized simultaneously, amplifying supply-chain fragility. The U.S. Central Command's blockade and Iran's counter-moves are creating a new normal where energy transit is contingent on great-power permission, with developing nations bearing the heaviest burden.

sections.title: Alliance Fractures and the Great Power Bargain: Taiwan, Trade, and Transatlantic Drift
sections.content: The Trump administration's simultaneous pursuit of bilateral deals with both adversaries and allies is restructuring global alliance architecture in ways that create new vulnerabilities. President Trump's May 2026 Beijing summit with Xi Jinping resulted in a de facto pause on a nearly $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, with Trump describing the arms sales as a 'very good negotiating chip.' This breaks a half-century bipartisan consensus and directly empowers Beijing to escalate coercion against Taipei. The strategic implications extend far beyond the Taiwan Strait: since nearly all advanced AI chips are manufactured in Taiwan, a Chinese blockade could cripple global technology supply chains and cost more than 10% of global GDP. In parallel, the U.S. tariff war is driving an unprecedented realignment among Western allies. Mexico, facing U.S. tariff pressure and the uncertain future of USMCA, signed an expanded free trade agreement with the European Union on May 22, which adds services and farm produce and includes $5.8 billion in EU investments under President Sheinbaum's Plan Mexico. The EU also finalized its Mercosur deal earlier this year, creating an Atlantic alternative to U.S.-centric trade. This is not a coincidence: it is a direct hedge against Washington's weaponization of market access—a strategy explicitly endorsed by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, who declared 2025 'the year of the tariff.' Meanwhile, the global rearmament cycle—driven by Japan's historic defense buildup, NATO's expansion amid Russian drone incursions into Romania, and U.S. calls for a $1.5 trillion defense budget—is being partially funded by these trade realignments. The House NDAA draft of $1.15 trillion leaves a $350 billion gap, signaling that even domestic U.S. fiscal priorities are strained by the multi-front posture. The combination of a paused Taiwan commitment and aggressive trade policy is eroding trust among Indo-Pacific allies, while incentivizing Beijing and Moscow to deepen their own partnership—as evidenced by North Korea's deployment of 15,000 troops to Ukraine in exchange for military technology and cash.

sections.title: Technology Domains: AI Governance, Cyber Force, and the Dual-Use Dilemma Across Theaters
sections.content: The convergence of artificial intelligence, cyber operations, and autonomous systems is reshaping warfare and governance across multiple regions simultaneously, creating both new escalation risks and coordination challenges. The United Nations is convening its Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva in July 2026, seeking to provide legitimacy to a fragmented landscape of national and regional initiatives (Bletchley, Seoul, Paris, New Delhi). Yet as the CFR analysis notes, these summits lack enforcement mechanisms and coherent standards. This fragmentation has real-world consequences: AI-driven border and asylum systems in Europe risk sending refugees back to unsafe countries, while cancer detection algorithms trained on light-skinned populations misdiagnose patients across the Global South. In parallel, the U.S. Senate is advancing a proposal to create a dedicated Cyber Force under the Army, with a projected budget of $16.5 billion and 10,000 personnel. The push is driven by 'new and escalating cyber threats on the battlefield,' according to Senator Gillibrand. These threats are not hypothetical: lessons from the Ukraine war—where North Korean troops operate alongside Russian forces and Ukrainian drones target Russian oil facilities—are informing SOCOM's push for 'fog computing' and smaller AI models that can operate at the tactical edge without cloud connectivity. Meanwhile, dual-use risks are multiplying. A Brazilian drug gang reportedly traveled to Ukraine to learn drone tactics, while AI researcher fears about synthetic biology and drone swarms at the FIFA World Cup highlight how non-state actors and adversary states can exploit commercial technologies. The Pope's encyclical on AI as a labor crisis akin to the Industrial Revolution underscores the governance vacuum. The NPT Review Conference's failure to reach consensus for the third consecutive cycle further weakens arms control frameworks, even as AI-enabled drone swarms and cyber attacks lower the threshold for conflict. The intersection of these technology trends means that a cyber attack originating from a proxy network could trigger a kinetic response across theaters—a risk that existing governance structures are not designed to manage.

key_developments: Iran reasserts unilateral control over Strait of Hormuz on May 30, demanding all vessels obtain IRGC permission, as U.S.-Iran deal remains elusive despite White House signaling imminent decision.
Philippines declares state of emergency due to oil/LNG shortages from Hormuz blockade, becoming first major economy to suffer acute energy crisis from the U.S.-Iran war.
War divides Filipino Muslims in Bangsamoro along sectarian lines (Shia-supporting vs. Sunni-critical), threatening community cohesion and echoing earlier Abraham Accords fractures.
Trump pauses $14 billion Taiwan arms package after Beijing summit, breaking bipartisan consensus and emboldening China to increase coercion; acting Navy secretary confirms 'pause.'
EU and Mexico sign expanded free trade agreement on May 22, adding services/farm produce and $5.8 billion in investments, as direct hedge against U.S. tariff uncertainty and USMCA fragility.
Israeli forces cross Litani River and encircle Nabatieh in southern Lebanon for first time since 2006, while simultaneously expanding Gaza occupation to 70% in violation of October 2025 ceasefire.
Russia drone strike on Romanian port city Galati on May 30 raises NATO-Russia direct confrontation risk, as Putin claims war 'nearing its end' and Zelenskyy warns of major aerial assault.
North Korean POWs captured in Ukraine (first confirmed evidence of 15,000 DPRK troops) become political pawns; human rights groups warn Geneva Convention violations endanger soldiers' families.
U.S. Senate amendment proposes creating a Cyber Force under the Army (projected 10,000 personnel, $16.5 billion) by 2027 NDAA, driven by escalating battlefield cyber threats.
U.N. blacklists Israel and Russia for sexual violence in conflict, verifying hundreds of cases across Gaza, West Bank, and Ukraine-occupied territories; both countries reject findings as biased.
House NDAA draft allocates $1.15 trillion but leaves $350 billion unfunded for Golden Dome, shipbuilding, and munitions, exposing fiscal strain of multi-front U.S. military posture.
Mexico offers to host Iran's World Cup training camp after Arizona withdrawal, as U.S.-Mexico bilateral relations deteriorate over security cooperation and tariff disputes.
outlook: Over the next 90 days, the global strategic environment will be defined by three intersecting dynamics. First, the U.S.-Iran war is unlikely to reach a comprehensive settlement before the U.S. midterm elections in November. Trump's insistence that he is 'not watching the clock' is contradicted by the electoral calendar, and Iran will likely continue to exploit the stalemate to consolidate control over the Strait of Hormuz. Expect further economic contagion in energy-importing developing nations across Southeast Asia and East Africa, potentially triggering additional states of emergency and protests that could topple vulnerable governments. Second, the erosion of U.S. alliance commitments—symbolized by the Taiwan arms pause, tariff-driven trade realignment (EU-Mexico, EU-Mercosur), and transactional security demands—will accelerate the formation of parallel blocs. Japan's constitutional revision and defense buildup, coupled with deepened Russia-North Korea military cooperation (nuclear tech for troops), will create a more polarized security architecture. The EU's pursuit of strategic autonomy, including its own defense industrial base and AI governance norms, may lead to open friction with NATO planning. Third, the technology domain will become a new flashpoint for escalation. The lack of consensus at the NPT Review Conference combined with AI-enabled autonomous systems and the proposed U.S. Cyber Force lowers the bar for non-kinetic attacks that could trigger retaliatory strikes. The July UN AI Governance Dialogue in Geneva is unlikely to produce binding commitments, leaving a regulatory vacuum that China and Russia may exploit for asymmetric advantage. Escalation risks are highest in the Taiwan Strait (where a Chinese coercion attempt could test U.S. resolve after the arms pause), on the NATO-Russia border (following the Romania drone incursion), and in southern Lebanon (where an Israeli assault on Nabatieh could draw in Hezbollah and trigger a wider war). The coming quarter will test whether traditional deterrence frameworks can survive the combination of resource fragmentation, technological disruption, and transactional diplomacy.
